title: Hong Kong's Digital Commons — the SaanSeoi Atlas
intro: SaanSeoi (山水) is an open-source project building a 'digital commons' for Hong Kong — shared, open data about the city's places and districts that anyone can use. Five short scenarios walk you through what a digital commons is, how the Atlas organises Hong Kong, and how an open API lets software (and AI agents) use the data. Choose what you would do — you get instant feedback. No account or AI key needed for this part.

scenarios.situation: Ka-yan wants a complete list of Hong Kong neighbourhoods for a school project. She finds three sources: a private map app that forbids copying its data, a government PDF that is hard to extract, and the SaanSeoi Atlas, an open dataset anyone may use and improve.
scenarios.question: Which source is a 'digital commons', and what makes it one?

options.text: The Atlas — open licence, anyone can use and improve it
options.feedback: Right. A commons is a resource the community shares and maintains together — like a public park, but made of data. Open licence + open contribution is what separates a commons from a product or a locked-up publication.

options.text: The map app — accuracy is what makes a commons
options.feedback: Accuracy is valuable, but it doesn't make something a commons. If the licence forbids reuse, the data belongs to the company, not the community — you can look, but you can't build on it.

options.text: The PDF — government data is automatically a commons
options.feedback: Public origin isn't enough. A PDF that is hard to extract and carries no clear reuse licence is 'published' but not really usable as shared infrastructure. A commons must be practically reusable, not just visible.

probe.question: Quick check: what are the two ingredients that make shared data a commons?

options.text: An open licence to reuse it, and a way for the community to contribute and correct it
Being free of charge and hosted on a government website
Being the most complete dataset available

bullets: Ka-yan needs a full list of HK neighbourhoods
SaanSeoi Atlas: open, anyone can improve it

scenarios.topic: Divisions: how the Atlas slices Hong Kong
scenarios.situation: The Atlas organises Hong Kong into division levels: 0 = SAR, 1 = Area (Kowloon, Hong Kong Island, New Territories), 2 = District (e.g. Yau Tsim Mong), 3 = Town, 4 = Macrohood (e.g. Mong Kok), 5 = Neighbourhood (e.g. Prince Edward), 6 = Microhood. Tommy wants to file 'Prince Edward' into this hierarchy.
scenarios.question: Where does Prince Edward belong, and why does a strict hierarchy matter?

options.text: Level 5, inside Mong Kok, inside Yau Tsim Mong
options.feedback: Exactly. Every division below District must sit inside exactly one district, so a program (or an AI agent) can walk up the chain from any small place to its district and area without guessing.

options.text: Level 2 — people call it a district in daily speech
options.feedback: Everyday speech is loose — people say 'district' for many neighbourhood-sized places. The Atlas fixes each name to one defined level precisely so that casual usage doesn't break the data. Prince Edward is a neighbourhood inside Mong Kok, inside the Yau Tsim Mong district.

options.text: Several levels at once — boundaries are fuzzy
options.feedback: Fuzzy boundaries are real, but if one name lived at several levels, queries like 'list all neighbourhoods in Yau Tsim Mong' would return duplicates and contradictions. The taxonomy rules (one level per division, one parent district) are what make the data computable.

probe.question: Quick check: in the Atlas taxonomy, how many districts (level 2) can a neighbourhood (level 5) belong to?

options.text: At least one — every division at level 3 or below must sit within a district
Zero — neighbourhoods are independent of districts
As many as the community votes for

bullets: Mong Kok is a level-4 macrohood

scenarios.topic: Why an API and not a spreadsheet?
scenarios.situation: The Atlas publishes its data through a web API with addresses like /v0/hk/places/{id}, /v0/hk/search?q=..., and /v0/divisions. Mei asks: 'Why not just publish one big spreadsheet for people to download?'
scenarios.question: What does an API give you that a downloadable spreadsheet does not?

options.text: Software can ask precise, live questions and get current data
options.feedback: Right. An API is a question-answering service: each URL is a specific question, and the answer is always drawn from the latest published snapshot. Spreadsheets go stale the moment they are downloaded, and every user must re-process the whole file.

options.text: An API keeps the data secret from outsiders
options.feedback: Backwards for a commons: the point of the Atlas API is to open the data to everyone, not to hide it. (An API key mainly helps the project manage load and abuse, not secrecy.)

options.text: No real difference — API is a fancier download link
options.feedback: A download gives you a frozen copy; an API answers specific questions on demand from live data. That difference is exactly what lets apps and AI agents build on the Atlas without each keeping their own stale copy.

probe.question: Quick check: what does the URL /v0/hk/search?q=tai+po most likely do?

options.text: Asks the Atlas to search Hong Kong places matching 'tai po' and return the results as data
Downloads the entire Atlas database
Edits the name of a place called Tai Po

bullets: Atlas serves data via a web API

scenarios.situation: The Atlas API describes itself with an OpenAPI specification: every endpoint lists its inputs, and every response has a declared shape — 200 means 'here is the place', 404 means 'no such place', 503 means 'the data snapshot is not ready yet'. Jason's app gets a 503 and he assumes the API is broken forever.
scenarios.question: What should Jason conclude from the 503, and why do declared response codes matter?

options.text: 503 is documented and temporary — wait and retry
options.feedback: Exactly. Because the API publishes its contract, every caller — human or AI agent — knows in advance what each status means and can respond sensibly: retry on 503, show 'not found' on 404, use the data on 200.

options.text: Any error code means the project is abandoned
options.feedback: Even the best services have moments when data is being republished or a request doesn't match anything. Maturity isn't 'no errors' — it's errors that are documented and predictable, which is what the OpenAPI spec provides.

options.text: Ignore codes — just check if the text looks like data
options.feedback: Guessing from the shape of the text is fragile and breaks silently. The status code is the API telling you exactly what happened — well-built software (and well-built agents) read the contract instead of guessing.

probe.question: Quick check: what is an OpenAPI specification?

options.text: A machine-readable contract listing an API's endpoints, inputs, and the exact shapes of its responses
A licence that makes an API free to use
The programming language the API is written in

bullets: 200 = place, 404 = not found, 503 = snapshot not ready

scenarios.topic: From open module to AI agent
scenarios.situation: A student team wants an AI tutor that answers questions about Hong Kong neighbourhoods. Option A: let the AI answer purely from its training memory. Option B: connect the AI to the Atlas API so it looks up divisions and places before answering.
scenarios.question: Why is Option B — grounding the agent in the open module — the stronger design?

options.text: B — answers become checkable against a shared, current source
options.feedback: Right. This is the whole experiment of wrapping open modules into agent platforms: the AI supplies language and reasoning, the commons supplies verifiable facts, and the two stay separate so each can improve independently.

options.text: A — a large model already memorised Hong Kong
options.feedback: Training memory is frozen at training time, blurry about small places, and impossible to audit. For a granular, changing city taxonomy, memory alone confidently invents details — grounding in live data is what makes answers trustworthy.

options.text: B — only because API calls make it faster
options.feedback: Speed isn't the point — an extra API call is usually slightly slower. The gain is accuracy and accountability: the agent can cite exactly which Atlas record its answer came from.

probe.question: Quick check: in the 'AI + open module' pattern, what does each side contribute?

options.text: The AI contributes language and reasoning; the open module contributes current, verifiable facts
The AI contributes facts; the module contributes conversation skills
Both sides contribute the same thing, for redundancy

bullets: Goal: an AI tutor on HK neighbourhoods
Option A: answer from training memory
Option B: look up the Atlas API first

finalCheck.question: A dataset counts as a digital commons when it is…

options.text: Openly licensed and community-maintained
Free to view on a website
Produced by a government body

finalCheck.question: In the Atlas taxonomy, Mong Kok (a macrohood) sits at…

options.text: Level 4, inside the Yau Tsim Mong district
Level 2, as its own district
Level 0, alongside the SAR

finalCheck.question: Compared with a downloadable file, an API…

options.text: Answers precise questions from the latest data on demand
Keeps the data private
Is only a fancier download link
Exactly what each endpoint accepts and what every response means
Who is allowed to use the API
How fast the API will respond

finalCheck.question: Grounding an AI agent in an open data module mainly buys you…

options.text: Checkable, current answers tied to a shared source
Faster responses
A smaller AI model

agent.name: Atlas Guide
agent.job: Answer questions about Hong Kong places and divisions, grounded in the SaanSeoi Atlas.
agent.knowledge: The Atlas division hierarchy and the open-commons ideas from Part A.
agent.tools: Live lookups against the Atlas demo API before every answer.
workflow: Ground the answer in matching records
agent.guardrails: If a place isn't in the snapshot, it says so — it never invents records.
agent.evaluation: Check its citations against the Atlas — every claim should trace to a record.
